tldr: By combining a tensegrity-based compliant continuum body with claw-based docking mechanisms, researchers developed "TeCoBot," a self-reconfigurable robot capable of both dexterous standalone manipulation/locomotion and multi-robot cooperative behaviors through shape-shifting.
hero_caption: Overview of the tensegrity continuum robot "TeCoBot." A single unit can extend, compress, bend omnidirectionally, and perform various locomotion and object manipulation tasks. Furthermore, multiple units can dock and reconfigure via claw-to-claw or claw-to-body connections to achieve advanced loco-manipulation tasks such as cooperative manipulation, pipe traversal, and table cleanup.
overview:
Conventional modular reconfigurable robots (MRRs) typically reconfigure by rearranging rigid, block-like modules. However, because their bodies lack structural compliance, they struggle to adapt to uneven terrain or object geometries and are prone to failure from minor docking misalignments. Consequently, their capabilities are often biased toward either locomotion or manipulation alone, making combined loco-manipulation difficult. On the other hand, continuum robots with flexible backbones conform well to environments, but they cannot dock or separate to reshape their overall multi-robot geometry.

To overcome these issues, the research team developed "TeCoBot," a novel modular robot featuring a compliant body made of stacked tensegrity structures with claws at both ends. Tensegrity combines compression-bearing rigid rods with tension-bearing elastic wires, resulting in a lightweight, robust structure that deforms smoothly and returns autonomously to its original shape. Endowing the robot's physical body with this passive compliance unlocks "embodied intelligence," allowing it to adapt naturally to external forces and contacts without relying on complex sensing and control.

In experiments, a single TeCoBot leveraged its ability to shrink, extend, and bend in all directions to perform rolling, inchworm locomotion, pipe climbing, and fruit grasping. Furthermore, three TeCoBots were shown to dock and reconfigure into chain, loop, H-shape, and branched morphologies by interlocking claws or gripping each other's bodies. Through these reconfigurations, the collective successfully lifted large balls that a single unit could not carry, clamped onto and traversed pipes, and cooperated to climb onto a desk, collect trash, and deposit it into a waste bin.
contributions: Created "TeCoBot," the world's first robot to combine a tensegrity continuum body with claw-based docking mechanisms, uniting compliance with modular reconfigurability.

Mechanically demonstrated the scalability of the stacked tensegrity architecture: even when stacking up to four modules in series, the required actuation force remains virtually constant at around 16–28 N.

Demonstrated not only rich multimodal locomotion (rolling, inchworm, pipe climbing, etc.) and object manipulation by a single unit, but also advanced loco-manipulation where multiple units autonomously and cooperatively alter their morphologies to complete complex tasks.

sections.heading: Introduction: Best of both worlds—rigid modules meet soft continuum bodies
sections.summary: This work tackles the challenge of combining the reconfigurability of modular robots with the compliance of continuum robots. To break down the rigidity of conventional MRR modules and the standalone isolation of continuum robots, the authors turned to tensegrity structures.
sections.details:
Robots capable of altering their morphologies and behaviors to match diverse tasks and environments are highly sought after for extreme exploration, disaster search-and-rescue, and space missions. Modular reconfigurable robots (MRRs) are prime candidates, as they can transform into snake, lattice, or legged configurations by rearranging modular units.

However, most existing MRRs rely on rigid cubic or spherical blocks. Lacking passive structural compliance, they cannot conform to unstructured terrain or the contours of grasped objects. Even minor positional misalignments often cause docking failures. As a result, they tend to specialize in either locomotion or manipulation, struggling to execute both at a high level.

Conversely, continuum robots—which bend gracefully like octopus arms or snakes—excel at maneuvering through confined spaces and contacting fragile objects due to their flexible backbones. However, they are traditionally built as monolithic, standalone systems and cannot separate or re-dock into entirely different geometric configurations in the field.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces "TeCoBot" (Tensegrity-based Continuum robot). It stacks icosahedron tensegrity modules—combining rigid carbon rods with stretchable elastic tendons—and equips both ends with multi-functional claws that handle both grasping and docking. Leveraging the embodied intelligence of tensegrity to absorb shocks while bearing substantial loads, the system allows robots to physically unite and evolve into new task-adaptive morphologies whenever needed.

sections.heading: TeCoBot hardware design: A clever blend of tensegrity and claw mechanisms
sections.summary: TeCoBot features a compliant body composed of stacked icosahedron tensegrity units made of 3D-printed elastic tendons and carbon rods. The claws at both ends act not only as end-effectors for grasping objects, but also as robust docking interfaces that lock onto another module's claws or body.
sections.details:
TeCoBot has a slim and lightweight profile, measuring 587 mm in total length, 110 mm in diameter, and weighing approximately 600 g (excluding batteries).

The core of the robot is a vertical stack of icosahedron tensegrity modules. A single module consists of six lightweight rigid carbon fiber rods (58 mm long, 2 mm diameter) and an integrated elastic tendon network 3D-printed from thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). These tensegrity units are connected via spacer disks, through which three actuation cables (high-strength 40-lb braided PE fishing line) pass at 120-degree intervals around the circumference. By independently pulling these three cables using three DC gearmotors with encoders in the base, the entire body can compress axially or bend smoothly across 360 degrees in any direction.

Both ends of the robot feature interchangeable modular three-finger claws. These claws utilize a self-locking worm gear mechanism, which mechanically maintains a firm grip on an object or a docked state without continuous motor power. Rubber sleeves on the claw tips enhance friction, enabling both symmetric claw-to-claw intermeshing and claw-to-body docking, where the claw grips another module's spacer disk or tensegrity mesh directly. In addition, passive roller wheels are embedded between the claw fingers to assist smooth rolling along the ground.

For onboard control, an ESP32 microcontroller and motor drivers are distributed in the bottom module, while an actuation battery (3-cell LiPo, 450 mAh) and a control battery (2-cell LiPo, 300 mAh) are housed in the top module, achieving fully wireless and untethered operation.

sections.heading: Mechanical characterization and modeling: Surprising scalability with constant actuation force
sections.summary: Tensile and bending tests across varying numbers of tensegrity stages and tendon thicknesses revealed that peak actuation forces remain virtually constant as modules are added. Kinematic modeling based on the constant curvature assumption also accurately predicts the robot's physical deformation.
sections.details:
To optimize TeCoBot's design, the research team conducted comprehensive mechanical characterization.

First, they evaluated the relationship between the cross-sectional size of the TPU tendons (1×2 mm, 2×2 mm, 3×2 mm) and the axial compression force and stroke. Thicker tendons increased stiffness, raising the maximum compression force from 17.5 N to 27.4 N; however, increasing it to 3×2 mm only yielded 30.9 N with diminished deformation range. Thus, 2×2 mm was chosen for the best balance between stiffness and required torque.

Most remarkably, module stacking demonstrated exceptional scalability. Increasing the number of tensegrity modules from 1 to 4 linearly quadrupled the maximum axial compression stroke from 60 mm to 260 mm. Despite this massive increase in displacement, the peak actuation force needed for full compression remained nearly constant between 23 and 28 N. The same held true for bending tests: while additional modules increased the maximum bending angle, the required actuation force remained unchanged at around 16–18 N. This proves that lengthening the robot body does not require upgrading to larger motors—a major mechanical advantage for modular robotics.

Next, the team measured the claw docking pull-off force, which determines connection reliability. In symmetric claw-to-claw docking, adding latex sleeves achieved a robust connection force of up to 42.9 ± 4.5 N. In claw-to-body docking (gripping the tensegrity mesh), the holding force reached 29.8 N at 1 A motor current, easily supporting the robot's own weight (~600 g = ~6 N) during lifting.

Finally, a kinematic model based on the constant curvature assumption was formulated. When validated against physical deformations across four representative cable-pulling patterns, tip position errors ranged from only 1.9 to 6.4 mm (0.8% to 3.0% of the backbone length), and 2D model silhouettes matched the real robot's shape with high fidelity.

(j) Comparison between the constant curvature model and physical 3D shapes across four representative poses, showing tip errors under 3% of the backbone length. (k) Top view showing cable actuation vectors combining to define the bending plane (angle $\phi$). (l) Projected model silhouettes closely matching experimental photographs on the bending plane.

sections.heading: Standalone versatility: From delicate picking to conquering rocks and pipes
sections.summary: Even as a standalone unit, TeCoBot performs delicate object manipulation within a 3D workspace by combining extension and omnidirectional bending. It also switches between multiple locomotion gaits—such as rolling, extension-compression, inchworm crawling, and pipe climbing—to navigate diverse environments.
sections.details:
A core strength of TeCoBot is that a single module already functions as a highly capable, self-contained robotic system.

In manipulation, fixing the base allows the three cable actuators to cover a broad 3D workspace. By coordinating claw opening/closing with extension and bending, TeCoBot easily performs delicate pick-and-place tasks—such as picking up soft grapes without crushing them and dropping them into narrow glass bottles.

For locomotion, the robot exhibits a remarkable variety of gaits:
- **Axial extension–compression**: Moving forward by alternately switching friction between the front and rear claws while extending and compressing the body.
- **Rolling**: Using the passive wheels between the claw fingers to shift its center of gravity and tumble forward at high speed.
- **Inchworm and crawling**: Arching and unarching the body to propel forward.
- **Pipe climbing**: Entering a vertical pipe and expanding radially against the inner walls to climb upward via friction.

When evaluating locomotion across eight outdoor and unstructured surfaces (smooth wood, grass, hay, gravel, rocks, etc.), axial extension achieved a steady 5 mm/s on smooth boards, but slipped on loose terrain like gravel and hay. However, switching to rolling allowed it to power through rocky and hay-covered terrain, achieving speeds up to 30 mm/s on wooden surfaces.

Furthermore, its Cost of Transport (CoT = Power / (Mass × Gravity × Velocity)) during rolling was measured at 7.4. This demonstrates significantly higher energy efficiency compared to conventional modular robots in the same class.

sections.heading: Cooperative multi-robot manipulation: Teaming up for heavy and multi-step tasks
sections.summary: Multiple TeCoBots mounted on a frame autonomously undocked and repositioned their claws to form four representative configurations (M1–M4). Working together, they lifted heavy spheres, uncorked test tubes to pour liquids, and linked into an elongated arm to retrieve distant objects.
sections.details:
When faced with objects too heavy for a single unit or tasks requiring multi-step coordination, TeCoBots collaborate to reshape their overall physical structure.

In experiments, three robots were mounted on a cubic frame equipped with docking stations. By releasing and relocating their claws, they reversibly transformed into four representative manipulation morphologies (M1–M4):
- **M1 (Three vertical modules)**: Three robots hung downward from the top of the frame. Bending inward synchronously, they enveloped and lifted a large ball 200 mm in diameter.
- **M2 (Two vertical, one horizontal module)**: One robot lowered to the ground horizontally. The two vertical robots held a test tube and pulled its cork stopper, after which the horizontal robot received the liquid and poured it into a beaker in a multi-step lab workflow.
- **M3 (One vertical, two horizontal modules)**: Two horizontal robots acted as a ground vise, firmly clamping a toilet paper roll from both sides. The vertical robot then pulled down and tore off paper sheets.
- **M4 (Three modules in serial chain)**: Three robots connected end-to-end via claws and bodies into an extended arm. This configuration reached across a wide gap to grab a distant bottle on a table and pull it back—a reach impossible for a single robot.

Transitions between M1 and M4 were achieved through sequences where robots released their claws from the frame, reoriented toward a new target station, and locked in place, demonstrating high morphology adaptability.

sections.heading: Cooperative multi-robot locomotion: Overcoming obstacles via chains, loops, and H-shapes
sections.summary: To navigate difficult obstacles such as flat terrain, pipes, and ducts, three robots transformed among serial chain (L1), loop-with-trailer (L2), H-shape (L3), and closed loop (L4) configurations. They bridged wide gaps and wrapped around large conduits to roll forward cooperatively.
sections.details:
Robots frequently encounter barriers like steps, narrow ducts, and conduits that a single unit cannot traverse. During transit, TeCoBots dynamically adapt their morphology by clamping claws together or gripping another module's body.

Four representative multi-robot locomotion morphologies (L1–L4) were demonstrated with three units:
- **L1 (Serial chain: ---)**: The middle robot repeatedly extends and compresses while the front and rear robots alternate contact friction, generating high thrust on flat terrain.
- **L2 (Loop with trailer: O-)**: Two front robots form a closed ring to envelop a payload (such as a large ball), while the trailing robot pushes it forward using an inchworm gait—ideal for transport.
- **L3 (H-shape: H)**: The robots clamp onto the exterior of a rectangular duct. The two side robots alternate gripping the duct walls while the central robot pushes and pulls, climbing along the duct without slipping off.
- **L4 (Closed loop: O)**: Three robots link end-to-end into a circular loop wrapping around a large cylindrical pipe. By coordinating internal bending and weight shifts, the loop rolls smoothly along the exterior of the pipe.

These configurations can transition flexibly into one another. For example, a serial chain (L1) can switch to a loop-with-trailer (L2) by having the lead robot detach while the remaining two form a loop, after which the detached unit re-clamps onto the loop's body.

Additionally, two linked robots successfully rolled across a wide crevasse that would swallow a single unit. Experiments also showed that scaling up to four modules unlocks further configurations, such as lizard-like crawling "H-shapes" and planar-translating "squares" (□).

sections.heading: Complex loco-manipulation: Autonomous teamwork from table cleanup to shelf sorting
sections.summary: As a benchmark connecting locomotion and manipulation seamlessly, the robots completed two real-world tasks: "Study Table Cleanup" and "Cabinet Organization." Three TeCoBots chained together, stood up vertically, and performed handovers to achieve complex multi-stage goals.
sections.details:
To demonstrate the full potential of TeCoBot, the team conducted physical experiments on two real-world scenarios requiring tightly coupled loco-manipulation.

**Task A: Study Table Cleanup**
The objective was to return a scattered pen to a pen holder on a 40-cm-high desk and discard crumpled paper into a floor trash bin.
1. Three robots formed a "Y-shape" on the floor. Two base robots braced against the ground and hoisted the front robot up onto the 40-cm-tall desk.
2. The robot on the desk crawled to the pen, picked it up, placed it into the holder, and then collected the paper scrap.
3. The two robots on the floor formed a serial chain and stood upright, performing a mid-air handover to receive the paper scrap from the desk robot.
4. The floor robot rotated and re-docked with the desk robot, forming a long three-robot chain bridging the desk and the floor. Extending directly over the trash bin, it dropped the paper squarely inside.

**Task B: Cabinet Organization**
The objective was to retrieve a motor from a parts bin on a shelf and stow it inside a nearby cabinet drawer.
1. Starting in a serial chain on the floor, one robot stood vertically and docked its claw into a wall-shelf bracket. Meanwhile, another robot pulled the drawer handle open.
2. The wall-mounted robot picked up the motor from the parts bin.
3. The two robots on the floor formed an upright chain to receive the motor from the wall robot via mid-air handover.
4. They placed the motor gently into the open drawer and used their body to push the drawer completely shut.

These sequences involved continuous physical contact and alignment demands that would cause rigid robots to jam or fail. The tensegrity structure's compliance naturally absorbed positional discrepancies and shocks, making the missions a success.

sections.heading: Discussion: Unlocking new robotic frontiers through embodied intelligence and reconfiguration
sections.summary: TeCoBot's breakthrough lies in unifying local body compliance with global multi-robot reconfigurability. While many demonstrations used teleoperation, autonomous vision-guided docking was also validated, establishing a strong foundation for fully autonomous task-adaptive morphology.
sections.details:
The primary academic contribution of this work is resolving the long-standing trade-off between local bodily compliance and global multi-robot reconfigurability within a single architecture.

The passive compliance provided by the tensegrity body conforms to gripped objects, disperses ground impacts, and physically absorbs alignment errors during docking. This embodied intelligence allows the hardware to handle environmental uncertainties without relying on heavy sensing arrays or millimetric feedback control loops. Meanwhile, the dual claw mechanisms allow the collective to freely alter its topology into chains, loops, or branches. As more modules are added, the combination of geometric topologies and individual continuum bending yields an exponential expansion in task adaptability.

While many cooperative demonstrations were teleoperated to highlight morphology capabilities, supplementary experiments validated that docking can be fully automated. The authors demonstrated both open-loop playback docking and closed-loop autonomous docking using a Raspberry Pi 5, an onboard camera, and ArUco markers. The robot successfully tracked the target, corrected misalignments, and interlocked claws autonomously.

Looking forward, integrating this hardware with high-level AI reasoning that automatically determines optimal morphologies from task and scene understanding will pave the way for autonomous collectives in extreme environments—from planetary exploration and disaster search-and-rescue to automated warehouse logistics.

sections.heading: Methods: Fabrication, control, and autonomous docking algorithms
sections.summary: The paper outlines detailed fabrication techniques, control circuitry, mechanical test setups, and autonomous docking strategies. Simulations also indicate that updating gear ratios can boost locomotion speeds by more than 2.4-fold.
sections.details:
Key technical specifications from the Methods and Supplementary Information include:

- **Fabrication**: Tensegrity tendons are 3D-printed flat from TPU using standard FDM printers. Carbon rods (2 mm outer diameter) are inserted into anchor sockets to assemble the 3D icosahedrons. Spacer disks and base modules are made of PLA, while high-stress components like cable spools and motor housings use polycarbonate (PC).
- **Communication and control**: Commands are sent via Wi-Fi from a PC-side ESP32-S3 transmitter to onboard ESP32-S3 receivers. Pololu micro metal gearmotors (380:1 gear ratio) are controlled through TB6612FNG motor drivers.
- **Claw actuation and sensing**: Dynamixel smart servos (XL330-M288-T) were used in claw characterization to monitor current and ensure consistent gripping force during pull-off tests. 9-axis IMUs (BNO085) at the base and tip measure body orientation, while an internal central cable and a ToF distance sensor (VL6180X) measure backbone displacement.
- **Speed enhancement analysis**: Currently, TeCoBot's axial extension speed (~5 mm/s) is bottlenecked by claw cycling time (7–10 s per open/close cycle). By changing the claw worm gear ratio from 380:1 to 30:1, locomotion speed can increase to ~12 mm/s (a 2.4-fold boost) without structural alterations. Upgrading the cable drive motors to higher RPM models could yield a 5.5-fold overall speed improvement.
- **Autonomous docking implementation**: An onboard Raspberry Pi 5 with a compact camera was mounted to the tip module. By tracking small and large ArUco markers on the partner robot, it switches from long-range coarse alignment to close-range precision alignment, executing a "Sense-Correct-Move" loop to achieve fully autonomous claw-to-claw docking.

takeaways: Endowing robots with passive tensegrity compliance (embodied intelligence) allows natural adaptation to unknown objects, rough terrain, and docking misalignments without excessive sensing or control.
Stacking tensegrity modules in series increases the stroke linearly while keeping the peak actuation force nearly constant, providing exceptional scalability for longer continuum bodies.

Uniting standalone versatility (multimodal locomotion and manipulation) with modular reconfiguration unlocks complex tasks—like payload transport, step climbing, and object handovers—that single robots cannot achieve.
The system offers strong practical extensibility; optimizing claw gear ratios and incorporating IMU feedback can multiply locomotion speeds several times over without structural redesigns.
limitations: Many of the complex real-world tasks (table cleanup and cabinet sorting) currently rely on human teleoperation; fully autonomous end-to-end planning that reasons over task demands to select optimal morphologies remains future work.
Claw actuation is slow (taking 7–10 seconds per open/close cycle) due to high-reduction (380:1) worm gears chosen for holding torque, creating a bottleneck in overall task execution time.
Axial extension locomotion slips on loose outdoor surfaces like gravel and grass, losing propulsion and making gait transitions necessary depending on the terrain.
